questions.stem: While auscultating a client with known left ventricular hypertrophy, the nurse hears an extra sound immediately before S1 that sounds like "Ten-nes-see." How should the nurse interpret this finding?
options: An S4 reflecting a stiff, noncompliant ventricle
An S3 reflecting acute fluid overload
A normal S1 from mitral and tricuspid closure
A normal S2 from aortic and pulmonic closure
rationales: The book describes S4 as an atrial gallop heard just before S1 that indicates a stiff ventricle, as seen in LVH.
S3 sounds like "Kentucky" and is heard just after S2, not before S1.
S1 is the normal "lub"; an added sound before it is not S1 itself.
S2 marks the end of systole and is heard at the base; it does not precede S1 as an extra sound.
questions.clue: The extra sound occurs just before S1 in a client with LVH.
questions.priority: Recognize an S4 gallop as a sign of a stiff ventricle.

questions.stem: During a cardiac assessment, the nurse hears an extra heart sound just after S2 with a "Ken-tuck-y" cadence. The nurse recognizes this finding most likely signals which problem?
options: A stiff ventricle from recent infarction
Fluid overload associated with heart failure
Normal closure of the semilunar valves
Normal onset of ventricular systole
rationales: A stiff ventricle produces S4, which is heard before S1, not after S2.
The book links S3, heard just after S2, to fluid overload in conditions such as CHF and valve insufficiency.
Semilunar valve closure is S2 itself, not an added sound following it.
S1 marks the beginning of systole; it is not an extra sound after S2.
questions.clue: The added sound follows S2 with a "Kentucky" cadence.
questions.priority: Link an S3 gallop to fluid overload.

questions.stem: A dehydrated client receives an IV fluid bolus. A student asks which cardiac concept is most directly increased by this intervention. Which response by the nurse is correct?
options: Afterload, the resistance the heart pushes against
Afterload, because the heart must squeeze faster
Preload, the volume filling the heart before it contracts
Preload, the pressure the heart faces during ejection
rationales: Afterload is the resistance to ejection, like a tightly tied balloon neck, not the incoming volume.
Afterload is defined by resistance after contraction starts, not by the rate of contraction.
The book defines preload as the volume before the squeeze, the blood coming into the heart; giving fluid adds to that volume.
This mixes the two concepts; pressure to push against during ejection describes afterload.
questions.clue: IV fluid adds volume returning to the heart.
questions.priority: Apply the preload versus afterload distinction to an intervention.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing auscultation findings for clients on a cardiac unit. For each description, indicate whether it describes an S3 or an S4 gallop.
rows: Heard just after S2
Heard just before S1 (pre-systolic)
Points to a stiff ventricle, as in LVH or MI
May signal fluid overload in CHF or cor pulmonale
Associated with aortic stenosis
rationales: The book places S3, the "Kentucky" ventricular gallop, just after S2.
S4, the "Tennessee" atrial gallop, is heard just before S1.
The book says S4 indicates a stiff ventricle, giving LVH and MI as examples.
The book links S3 to fluid overload in conditions such as CHF, pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale.
The book lists aortic stenosis as associated with S4.
questions.clue: The timing of the extra sound relative to S1 and S2 separates S3 from S4.
questions.priority: Classify gallops by timing and the condition they suggest.

questions.stem: The nurse auscultates the heart of a client recently diagnosed with pulmonary embolism. Which statements about the client's S2 heart sound are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: It is produced by closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves
It is heard best at the apex, 5th ICS, midclavicular line
It is heard best at the base, 2nd ICS, right and left sternal borders
It may be louder in this client because of the pulmonary embolism
It marks the beginning of systole
It is produced by closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves
rationales: The book describes S2 ("dub") as closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves.
The apex at the 5th ICS, midclavicular line, is where the book says S1 is heard best.
The book says S2 is heard best at the base, 2nd ICS at the right and left sternal borders.
The book notes that S2 is louder in clients with PE.
S2 marks the end of systole and start of diastole; S1 marks the beginning of systole.
Mitral and tricuspid closure produces S1, not S2.
questions.clue: The client has a pulmonary embolism, which the book links to a louder S2.
questions.priority: Locate and interpret S2 correctly during cardiac auscultation.

questions.stem: A client with a penetrating chest wound becomes hypotensive with distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds. What is the nurse's first action?
options: Reassess vital signs again in 30 minutes
Position flat and continue routine monitoring
Request a routine echocardiogram for the morning
Call for emergency help, as this is a true emergency
rationales: Tamponade requires urgent diagnosis and treatment; delaying reassessment wastes critical time.
The book advises HOB 30-45 degrees if stable and emergency escalation, not routine monitoring.
The book stresses urgent diagnosis and treatment; a deferred study is inappropriate.
Hypotension, JVD and muffled heart sounds are Beck's triad; the book's first nursing priority for tamponade is to call for help.
questions.clue: Beck's triad appears after penetrating chest trauma.
questions.priority: Escalate suspected cardiac tamponade as an emergency.

questions.stem: The nurse suspects cardiac tamponade in a post-trauma client. Which additional assessment finding best supports this suspicion?
options: Systolic BP falls more than 10 mm Hg on inspiration
Widening pulse pressure with bounding pulses
Bradycardia with a regular rhythm
A narrowed mediastinum on chest x-ray
rationales: The book lists pulsus paradoxus, a drop of more than 10 mm Hg in BP during inspiration, as a sign of tamponade.
The book lists a narrow pulse pressure, not a widening one, in tamponade.
Tachycardia, not bradycardia, is listed among tamponade signs.

Mediastinal width is not a reliable tamponade sign. Widening may suggest major vascular injury; a chronic large effusion may enlarge the cardiac silhouette. Suspected tamponade needs urgent echocardiographic/clinical assessment.
questions.clue: Blood pressure changes with the respiratory cycle.
questions.priority: Identify pulsus paradoxus as a tamponade finding.

questions.stem: A hemodynamically stable client with suspected cardiac tamponade is awaiting pericardiocentesis. How should the nurse position the client?
options: Supine and flat with legs elevated
Head of bed elevated 30-45 degrees
Prone to reduce pressure on the heart
Left lateral with head of bed flat
rationales: This is not the position the book recommends for a stable tamponade client.
The book's nursing priorities state HOB 30-45 degrees if the client is stable.
Prone positioning is not mentioned and would hinder monitoring and the procedure.
The book specifies head elevation of 30-45 degrees, not a flat side-lying position.
questions.clue: The client is stable while awaiting the procedure.
questions.priority: Position a stable tamponade client correctly.

questions.stem: After blunt chest trauma, an awake client has BP 84/60 mmHg, JVD and muffled heart sounds. The team suspects tamponade. Which immediate actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Wait for a routine echocardiography appointment.
Provide oxygen as needed and alert the airway team if breathing fails, with hemodynamic preparation.
Administer a diuretic without clarifying the order despite hypotension and suspected tamponade.
Prepare for urgent definitive drainage through the trauma/cardiac team.
Continuously reassess vital signs, mental status, ECG and oxygenation.
Wait for another routine vital-sign cycle before calling for help.
rationales: Incorrect. Tamponade with shock physiology is an emergency; a routine delay is unsafe.
Correct. Provide respiratory support according to need. Positive-pressure ventilation can precipitate collapse by reducing venous return; reserve it for necessity with expert hemodynamic preparation.
Incorrect. Reducing preload may worsen hypotension; clarify the order urgently. Positioning is individualized to perfusion and trauma precautions rather than a universal HOB angle.
Correct. Definitive drainage must be coordinated urgently; the method depends on trauma context and expertise.
Correct. Close monitoring detects deteriorating perfusion while definitive care is arranged.
Incorrect. Summon emergency help promptly rather than delaying escalation.
questions.clue: Beck's triad (hypotension, JVD, muffled heart sounds) after chest trauma.
questions.priority: Plan emergency care for suspected cardiac tamponade.
questions.takeaway: Unstable tamponade needs urgent decompression and carefully coordinated perfusion/airway support.

questions.stem: A client with suspected cardiac tamponade is awaiting pericardiocentesis. Which equipment should the nurse make sure is at the bedside?
options: A sequential compression device for DVT prevention
A bedside commode to limit exertion
A crash cart and defibrillator
An incentive spirometer for lung expansion
rationales: DVT prevention is not the immediate safety concern the book lists for tamponade.
Toileting equipment does not address the risk of sudden deterioration.
The book's nursing priorities include keeping a crash cart and defibrillator at the bedside.
Lung expansion is not the priority; the book focuses on readiness for emergency resuscitation.
questions.clue: Tamponade can deteriorate suddenly while the client waits for the procedure.
questions.priority: Keep emergency equipment ready for a client at risk of arrest.

questions.stem: A client arrives in the emergency department reporting crushing chest pain that began 30 minutes ago. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Draw a lipid panel to assess cardiac risk
Schedule an exercise stress test
Obtain a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of arrival
Start a high-intensity statin by mouth
rationales: Lipids do not guide immediate ACS diagnosis or reperfusion decisions.
Stress testing is not part of the immediate ACS priorities the book lists.
The book states the priority in ACS is a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes.
Statins are post-MI therapy; the ECG comes first to identify STEMI.
questions.clue: Acute chest pain suggests acute coronary syndrome.
questions.priority: Prioritize a rapid 12-lead ECG in suspected ACS.

questions.stem: A client with an inferior MI has ST elevation in V4R and a low blood pressure. Which prescribed medication should the nurse question?
options: IV fluid bolus to support blood pressure
Dobutamine infusion for inotropic support
Chewable aspirin to inhibit platelets
Sublingual nitroglycerin for chest pain
rationales: The book recommends IV fluids for right ventricular infarct.
Positive inotropes such as dobutamine are recommended for right ventricular infarct.
Aspirin is given in MI unless contraindicated; nothing in the stem contraindicates it.
The book says to avoid nitrates in right ventricular infarct because they worsen already low preload.
questions.clue: ST elevation in V4R with hypotension indicates right ventricular infarct.
questions.priority: Avoid preload reducers in right ventricular MI.

questions.stem: A client with NSTEMI reports taking sildenafil earlier today. Before giving nitroglycerin, what is the nurse's main concern?
options: Dangerous hypotension from the nitrate and PDE-5 inhibitor combination
Severe bradycardia from unopposed alpha stimulation
Increased bleeding from combined platelet inhibition
Rebound hypertension once the nitrate wears off
rationales: The book warns that nitrates combined with PDE-5 inhibitors such as sildenafil can cause dangerous hypotension.
Unopposed alpha stimulation relates to beta-blockers with cocaine, not nitrates with sildenafil.
Bleeding risk is not the interaction the book describes for nitrates and sildenafil.
The book describes hypotension, not rebound hypertension, with this combination.
questions.clue: The client took sildenafil before nitrate therapy.
questions.priority: Recognize the nitrate and PDE-5 inhibitor interaction.

questions.stem: The emergency department nurse is caring for four clients with chest pain. Which client should the nurse see first?
options: A client whose exertional chest pain stopped when he rested in triage
A client with chest pain for 30 minutes, diaphoresis, shortness of breath and ST elevation
A client with known variant angina who is pain free and asking about calcium channel blockers
A client whose earlier chest pain has resolved and whose first troponin was not elevated
rationales: Chest pain that ceases when exertion stops matches the book's description of stable angina.
Pain over 20 minutes with diaphoresis, shortness of breath and ST elevation are STEMI signs; the book labels STEMI an emergency needing immediate reperfusion.
This client is pain free; variant angina is treated with CCBs or NTG, and no acute change is described.
The client is pain free now; the book notes troponin does not rise in unstable angina, and STEMI is the more urgent problem.
questions.clue: ST elevation with ongoing pain, diaphoresis and shortness of breath.
questions.priority: Prioritize the client with STEMI for immediate reperfusion.

questions.stem: A nonpregnant adult presents to a rural hospital with STEMI symptoms that began 2 hours ago. The team estimates first-medical-contact-to-PCI time will exceed 120 minutes and confirms no fibrinolysis contraindications. Which reperfusion plan should the nurse anticipate?
options: Observe on telemetry and repeat troponin before selecting reperfusion.
Give aspirin and arrange elective PCI next week.
Treat as NSTEMI because a catheterization laboratory is unavailable.
Administer prescribed fibrinolysis promptly and arrange immediate transfer for PCI-capable care.
rationales: Incorrect. STEMI reperfusion must not wait for serial biomarkers when the ECG and presentation establish the diagnosis.
Incorrect. Aspirin is important but does not replace timely reperfusion.
Incorrect. Availability of a catheterization laboratory does not change STEMI into NSTEMI.
Correct. With onset under 12 hours, excessive PCI delay and no contraindications, fibrinolysis followed by immediate transfer is an appropriate strategy.
questions.clue: STEMI in a facility without a cath lab.
questions.priority: Coordinate reperfusion and transfer for STEMI.
questions.takeaway: STEMI reperfusion choice depends on symptom timing, anticipated PCI delay and contraindications.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews new metoprolol prescriptions for clients with ACS. Which prescriptions require clarification before administration? Select all that apply.
options: A client with chest pain, agitation and hypertension during active cocaine intoxication
A client 12 hours after MI with HR 84/min and BP 134/82 mm Hg
A client with a PR interval of 0.28 seconds and no pacemaker
A client with active bronchospasm from severe asthma
A client with BP 152/94 mm Hg and HR 96/min
A client with acute decompensated heart failure and pulmonary edema
rationales: Active intoxication warrants clarification of a pure beta-blocker prescription and management under the acute stimulant/ACS protocol. A remote cocaine history alone does not establish a contraindication.
The book recommends starting a beta-blocker within 24 hours after MI when there is no bradycardia or hypotension.
The book lists AV block with a PR interval over 0.24 s and no pacer as a reason to avoid beta-blockers.
Active bronchospasm from severe asthma or COPD is a listed reason to avoid beta-blockers.
An elevated BP and heart rate are not among the book's contraindications.
The book lists acute decompensated heart failure and pulmonary edema as a reason to avoid beta-blockers.
questions.clue: Each client is checked against the book's list of beta-blocker contraindications.
questions.priority: Prevent harm by questioning contraindicated beta-blocker orders.
questions.takeaway: Clarify beta-blocker orders when current intoxication, significant conduction delay, active bronchospasm or acute decompensated heart failure creates a safety concern.

questions.stem: An inferior MI involves the right ventricle. BP is 82/50 mm Hg, the lungs are clear, and the cardiology team identifies low preload. After an initial small fluid bolus with reassessment, cardiac output remains low. The team prescribes cautious further fluid assessment and dobutamine with concurrent vasopressor support if needed. Classify these actions for the current plan.
rows: Give a small prescribed isotonic fluid bolus and reassess perfusion and lung findings.
Administer prescribed dobutamine with close BP monitoring and hemodynamic support.
Give sublingual nitroglycerin while BP remains 82/50 mm Hg.
Give IV furosemide despite low preload and clear lungs.
Give IV morphine without clarifying the order despite persistent hypotension.
rationales: Cautious preload optimization may help RV infarction; avoid indiscriminate fluid loading.
Inotropic support may be used for persistent low output after preload assessment; dobutamine can lower BP, so it is not a stand-alone universal treatment for shock.
Nitrates can further reduce preload and BP in this hypotensive client.
Diuresis may worsen low preload when congestion is absent.
Morphine may worsen hypotension and requires individualized analgesia assessment.
questions.clue: ST elevation in V4R with hypotension signals right ventricular infarct.
questions.priority: Support preload and avoid preload reducers in right ventricular MI.
questions.takeaway: Hypotensive RV infarction requires reassessed preload, perfusion support and urgent reperfusion; avoid automatic large fluid or drug rules.

questions.stem: A client is tense and tearful as the nurse prepares to remove a femoral sheath after PCI. The client says, "I'm scared this is going to hurt." Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Address the client's pain and anxiety before and during sheath removal
Give sublingual nitroglycerin to help the client relax
Remove the sheath quickly before the anxiety builds
Limit direct pressure to 5 minutes to shorten the discomfort
rationales: The book warns of a vasovagal response during sheath removal and directs the nurse to manage pain and anxiety.
The book says to hold nitrates (preload reducers) during sheath removal because of hypotension risk.
Rushing ignores the client's fear and does not reduce the vasovagal risk the book describes.
Compression is maintained until hemostasis according to the ordered access-site protocol; a fixed five-minute limit risks bleeding.
questions.clue: The client is frightened and in pain right before sheath removal.
questions.priority: Manage anxiety and pain to reduce the vasovagal response.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old athlete is diagnosed with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with asymmetric septal hypertrophy. Which risk should the nurse emphasize in teaching?
options: Progressive enlargement of the ventricles
Sudden death from ventricular arrhythmias
Blood stasis leading to thrombus formation
Recurrent pulmonary infection from impaired immunity
rationales: Enlarged ventricles describe dilated cardiomyopathy, not HCM.
The book links HCM to sudden death in young athletes from ventricular arrhythmias due to asymmetric septal hypertrophy.
Blood stasis is listed as a feature of dilated cardiomyopathy.

Impaired immunity and recurrent infection are not defining consequences of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Cardiomyopathy prognosis varies by cause, stage and treatment; a universal one-to-two-year survival estimate is inappropriate.
questions.clue: A young athlete has asymmetric septal hypertrophy.
questions.priority: Teach the sudden-death risk in HCM.

questions.stem: An echocardiogram shows enlarged ventricles, atrial enlargement and impaired systolic function. The nurse recognizes which type of cardiomyopathy?
options: Restrictive cardiomyopathy, the least common type
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with rapid contraction
Dilated cardiomyopathy, the most common type
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with impaired relaxation
rationales: Restrictive disease has stiff ventricles with preserved contraction.
HCM features thickened walls and rapid contraction, not impaired systolic function.
The book lists enlarged ventricles, impaired systolic function and atrial enlargement as features of dilated cardiomyopathy, the most common type.
Impaired relaxation with thickened walls describes HCM, not enlarged ventricles.
questions.clue: The ventricles are enlarged and systolic function is impaired.
questions.priority: Differentiate cardiomyopathy types by their features.

questions.stem: The nurse is taking a history from a client newly diagnosed with cardiomyopathy. Which lifestyle question is most relevant according to the assessment guidance?
options: "How many hours of sleep do you get?"
"How much caffeine do you have each day?"
"How often do you eat fast food meals?"
"How much alcohol do you usually drink?"
rationales: Sleep is not among the lifestyle factors the book lists for cardiomyopathy.
Caffeine intake is not included in the book's cardiomyopathy assessment.
Diet pattern is not a lifestyle factor named in the book's assessment.
The book lists assessing patterns of alcohol consumption under lifestyle factors for cardiomyopathy.
questions.clue: The history focuses on cardiomyopathy risk factors.
questions.priority: Assess modifiable contributors to cardiomyopathy.

questions.stem: A client with cardiomyopathy is starting several medications. Which statements by the nurse correctly describe the expected drug effects? Select all that apply.
options: "Hydralazine will mainly dilate your veins."
"The beta-blocker will slow your heart rate and lower your blood pressure."
"Digoxin strengthens contractions by inhibiting the sodium-potassium pump."
"Verapamil works by increasing calcium entry into heart muscle cells."
"Nitrates mainly dilate your veins."
"Digoxin weakens contractions so your heart can rest."
rationales: The book states hydralazine dilates arteries; it is nitrates that primarily dilate veins.
The book says beta-blockers decrease myocardial oxygen demand, resulting in a slow HR and reduced BP.
The book says digoxin increases contraction force by inhibiting Na+/K+-ATPase, raising intracellular calcium.
The book says calcium channel blockers such as verapamil block calcium influx.
The book states nitrates primarily dilate veins.
The book describes digoxin as increasing, not reducing, the force of contraction.
questions.clue: Each statement names a drug from the cardiomyopathy treatment list.
questions.priority: Teach accurate mechanisms of cardiomyopathy medications.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing notes for clients with cardiomyopathy. For each finding, indicate the type of cardiomyopathy it describes.
rows: Enlarged ventricles with blood stasis
Thickened ventricular walls with rapid contraction
Stiff ventricles with preserved contraction
Impaired relaxation and a risk of sudden death in young athletes
Restrictive filling physiology with nondilated ventricles and no marked wall hypertrophy
rationales: The book lists enlarged ventricles and blood stasis under dilated cardiomyopathy.
Thickened walls and rapid contraction are characteristics of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Stiff ventricles, impaired filling and preserved contraction describe restrictive cardiomyopathy.
The book lists impaired relaxation for HCM and links it to sudden death in young athletes.

Restrictive physiology causes impaired ventricular filling; this row’s nondilated ventricles and absence of marked hypertrophy distinguish it from the other supplied patterns. Prognosis depends on the underlying cause and severity.
questions.clue: Wall size, contraction and filling patterns differ by type.
questions.priority: Differentiate the three types of cardiomyopathy.
questions.takeaway: Use ventricular geometry, wall thickness and filling physiology to distinguish cardiomyopathy patterns; do not use a fixed survival estimate.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old female client is being evaluated for newly diagnosed cardiomyopathy. Along with her alcohol intake, which assessment is most important for the nurse to include?
options: Her history of seasonal pollen allergies
Her usual number of hours of sleep
Whether she is currently pregnant
Her daily caffeine intake
rationales: Pollen allergies are not listed; the book asks about hypersensitive reactions to medications.
Sleep is not among the factors the book lists for cardiomyopathy assessment.
The book directs the nurse to determine whether female clients are pregnant.
Caffeine is not one of the lifestyle factors the book names; alcohol is.
questions.clue: A woman of childbearing age with new cardiomyopathy.
questions.priority: Include pregnancy status in the cardiomyopathy history.

questions.stem: A client reports waking at night short of breath and needing three pillows to sleep. Crackles and pink frothy sputum are present. The nurse recognizes these findings as consistent with which condition?
options: Left-sided heart failure with pulmonary congestion
Right-sided heart failure with systemic congestion
Restrictive cardiomyopathy with preserved contraction
Hypertensive urgency without organ involvement
rationales: The book lists PND, orthopnea, crackles and pink frothy sputum under left-sided failure ("Left = Lungs").
Right-sided failure shows peripheral edema and JVD, with minimal pulmonary signs.
These pulmonary findings are described under left-sided heart failure, not restrictive disease.
Pulmonary edema signals organ involvement and is not described as urgency.
questions.clue: Orthopnea, PND and crackles point to the lungs.
questions.priority: Differentiate left- from right-sided heart failure.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure is comfortable at rest but becomes markedly short of breath walking to the bathroom. Which NYHA class does the nurse document?
options: Class I
Class III
Class II
Class IV
rationales: Class I means no symptoms with normal activity.
The book defines Class III as marked symptoms with minimal activity.
Class II means mild symptoms with moderate activity.
Class IV means symptoms are present even at rest, which this client denies.
questions.clue: Symptoms are marked with minimal activity but absent at rest.
questions.priority: Classify functional status using NYHA classes.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure and new oliguria has a proposed dopamine infusion at 2 mcg/kg/min specifically “to protect kidney function.” Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Begin it because low-dose dopamine reliably prevents kidney injury.
Explain that a higher dopamine dose is needed for kidney protection.
Clarify the indication and assess perfusion, congestion and other causes of oliguria.
Delay all oliguria assessment until the next routine laboratory panel.
rationales: Incorrect. Renal vasodilator effects have not established kidney-protective clinical benefit.
Incorrect. Increasing dopamine does not establish a kidney-protection indication and introduces other hemodynamic effects.
Correct. Low-dose dopamine should not be normalized as renal-protective therapy; clarify the plan and evaluate the cause of reduced output.
Incorrect. New oliguria needs timely clinical assessment.
questions.clue: The infusion rate is 2 mcg/kg/min.
questions.priority: Match dopamine dose ranges to receptor effects.
questions.takeaway: A receptor effect does not prove kidney protection; investigate oliguria and use an evidence-based individualized plan.

questions.stem: A client is admitted with dyspnea, orthopnea and edema. Which diagnostic findings would support a diagnosis of heart failure? Select all that apply.
options: Normal basic labs, which rule out heart failure
BNP of 450 pg/mL
BNP of 40 pg/mL
Chest x-ray showing cardiomegaly and pleural effusion
ECG showing left ventricular hypertrophy
rationales: The book states that normal labs do not exclude heart failure.
The book lists a BNP of 100 pg/mL or higher as a heart failure finding.
A BNP of 40 pg/mL is below the book's 100 pg/mL threshold.
The book lists cardiomegaly, pulmonary edema and pleural effusion as chest x-ray findings.
The book notes the ECG in heart failure may show arrhythmia or LVH.
questions.clue: Classic heart failure symptoms need diagnostic confirmation.
questions.priority: Interpret basic heart failure diagnostics.

questions.stem: A client with right-sided heart failure has pitting edema of both legs, JVD and ascites. For each nursing action, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated.
rows: Elevate the client's legs
Keep the legs dependent to help fluid drain
Support sodium restriction as prescribed
Infuse a large IV fluid bolus to improve output
Monitor daily weight for gain
rationales: The book's caution for right-sided failure says to elevate the legs.
Dependent positioning is the opposite of the book's advice to elevate the legs.
The book lists sodium restriction, used cautiously, for right-sided failure.
The book says to manage fluids carefully in right-sided failure; a large bolus adds to fluid overload.
Weight gain is a listed symptom of right-sided failure, so tracking it is appropriate.
questions.clue: Peripheral edema, JVD and ascites point to systemic congestion.
questions.priority: Provide comfort measures that reduce systemic congestion.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four clients with heart failure. Which client should the nurse see first?
options: A client with Class II HF who has mild dyspnea climbing stairs
A client with right-sided HF who has stable ankle edema and nocturia
A client with HF who reports anorexia and fatigue at breakfast
A client with left-sided HF who is newly restless and confused with pink frothy sputum
rationales: Class II means mild symptoms with moderate activity; this is expected and stable.
Peripheral edema and nocturia are expected right-sided findings and are described as stable.
Anorexia and fatigue are listed right-sided symptoms but are not acute.
The book lists pink frothy sputum, restlessness and confusion under left-sided failure with pulmonary congestion; new changes signal worsening.
questions.clue: New restlessness and confusion with pink frothy sputum.
questions.priority: See first the client with worsening pulmonary congestion.

questions.stem: A client with pulmonary hypertension has improved on inhaled nitric oxide, and the team plans to stop it. What should the nurse anticipate?
options: Abrupt discontinuation once oxygenation improves
Switching directly to an IV beta-blocker
Increasing the dose before stopping it
A slow taper to avoid rebound pulmonary hypertension
rationales: Abrupt stopping risks rebound pulmonary hypertension, per the book.
No such substitution is described for nitric oxide withdrawal.
The book calls for a slow taper, not a dose increase.
The book states inhaled nitric oxide should be tapered off slowly to avoid rebound pulmonary hypertension.
questions.clue: Inhaled nitric oxide is being discontinued.
questions.priority: Prevent rebound pulmonary hypertension during weaning.

questions.stem: A client with severe pulmonary arterial hypertension is started on a continuous IV epoprostenol infusion. The family asks why this drug was chosen. Which response is accurate?
options: It dilates pulmonary arteries in the selected PAH treatment plan
It mainly prevents clots in the pulmonary vessels
It mainly removes excess fluid from the body
It mainly opens the airways to ease breathing
rationales: Epoprostenol is a prostacyclin-pathway therapy that reduces pulmonary vascular resistance; selected severe PAH clients may gain functional and survival benefit. Do not claim superiority over every modern therapy without a defined comparison.
Clot prevention is the role of anticoagulants such as warfarin.
Fluid removal is the role of diuretics such as furosemide.
Bronchodilators such as albuterol are listed for breathing support.
questions.clue: The drug is IV epoprostenol for severe disease.
questions.priority: Explain the purpose of prostacyclin therapy.

questions.stem: A client's echocardiogram suggests pulmonary hypertension. Which test does the nurse anticipate to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Thyroid-stimulating hormone level
Right-heart catheterization with hemodynamic measurements
HIV antibody screening
Pulmonary function testing
rationales: TSH is listed among tests to identify underlying causes, not to confirm the diagnosis.

Right-heart catheterization confirms elevated mean pulmonary artery pressure and helps classify PH using wedge pressure and PVR. Elevated PVR is part of precapillary classification, not a requirement for every PH subtype.
HIV testing helps find an associated cause rather than confirm pressures.
PFTs help evaluate lung-related causes but do not confirm pulmonary pressures.
questions.clue: The diagnosis needs confirmation after an abnormal echo.
questions.priority: Identify the confirmatory test for pulmonary hypertension.

questions.stem: A client with pulmonary arterial hypertension says, "Every time I get short of breath I panic and think I'm going to die." Which nursing approach is best?
options: Tell the client that panic is not related to the condition
Monitor the client's anxiety, offer support and help minimize stress
Encourage the client to push through activity to build tolerance
Move the conversation to the medication schedule as a distraction
rationales: Dismissing the feeling is not supportive and ignores the book's psychosocial guidance.
The book's psychosocial assessment for PAH says to monitor anxiety, provide support and minimize stress.
Pushing through dyspnea adds stress and cardiac workload, which the goal of care seeks to reduce.
Changing the subject avoids the client's concern instead of providing support.
questions.clue: The client describes panic with shortness of breath.
questions.priority: Support the psychosocial needs of a client with PAH.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client with pulmonary arterial hypertension about prescribed medications. Which drugs does the nurse explain promote selective pulmonary vasodilation? Select all that apply.
options: Furosemide
Sildenafil
Warfarin
Riociguat
Tadalafil
Hydrochlorothiazide
rationales: The book lists furosemide as a diuretic that reduces fluid overload.
The book lists sildenafil among PAH-specific drugs that promote selective pulmonary vasodilation.
The book lists warfarin as an anticoagulant that prevents clots.
Riociguat is listed as a PAH-specific drug that promotes selective pulmonary vasodilation.
Tadalafil is listed as a PAH-specific drug that promotes selective pulmonary vasodilation.
The book lists hydrochlorothiazide as a diuretic, not a pulmonary vasodilator.
questions.clue: The question asks for selective pulmonary vasodilators.
questions.priority: Match PAH drugs to their actions.

questions.stem: A client with obesity and obstructive sleep apnea is diagnosed with pulmonary hypertension and asks, "How did I get this?" Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
options: "Conditions that lower your oxygen level, like sleep apnea and obesity, can lead to it."
"It is idiopathic, so it cannot be linked to anything in your history."
"It was most likely caused by a viral infection of your heart muscle."
"It comes from fatty buildup in the arteries of your legs."
rationales: The book says secondary forms result from hypoxemia-related conditions such as COPD, obesity, high altitude and sleep apnea.
Idiopathic PAH has no known cause, but this client has hypoxemia-related conditions the book links to secondary forms.
Viral infection of the heart muscle describes myocarditis, not a cause of pulmonary hypertension in this section.
Atherosclerosis in the leg arteries describes peripheral arterial occlusive disease.
questions.clue: The client has obesity and sleep apnea.
questions.priority: Link modifiable hypoxemia-related conditions to secondary pulmonary hypertension.

questions.stem: A client has a BP of 210/124 mm Hg with new confusion and papilledema. Which plan of care does the nurse anticipate?
options: Discharge home on oral clonidine with follow-up
Observation with oral captopril over 48 hours
Hospital admission with an IV agent such as nicardipine
Recheck BP in one week at the clinic
rationales: Oral outpatient therapy is the book's approach for urgency, not emergency.
Gradual oral reduction is for urgency without target organ damage.
Papilledema and encephalopathy are target organ damage; the book directs immediate hospitalization and IV antihypertensives.
Target organ damage requires immediate hospital treatment.
questions.clue: Confusion and papilledema indicate end-organ damage.
questions.priority: Distinguish hypertensive emergency and its management.

questions.stem: A nonpregnant adult has hypertensive encephalopathy. Stroke and aortic dissection have been excluded. IV nicardipine is prescribed with an initial target of no more than a 25% reduction in mean arterial pressure during the first hour. Which action follows this plan?
options: Reduce BP immediately to below 120/80 mm Hg.
Reduce the starting mean arterial pressure by at least 50%.
Withhold the infusion for 24 hours.
Titrate cautiously without exceeding the prescribed first-hour MAP reduction.
rationales: Incorrect. Immediate normalization may compromise organ perfusion.
Incorrect. A 50% fall exceeds the prescribed initial limit.
Incorrect. Acute organ injury requires prompt monitored treatment.
Correct. This respects the specified target while monitoring neurologic status and perfusion. Other hypertensive emergencies may require different targets.
questions.clue: The client is in the first hour of IV treatment.
questions.priority: Avoid lowering BP too fast in hypertensive emergency.
questions.takeaway: Use the diagnosis-specific ordered BP target; avoid abrupt normalization.

questions.stem: A nonpregnant adult has repeat BP 186/122 mm Hg after proper measurement. Clinical evaluation finds no acute target-organ injury. Which plan should the nurse anticipate?
options: Timely review of the oral regimen, adherence and follow-up, with gradual controlled reduction.
ICU admission solely for immediate IV BP normalization.
An IV infusion to lower MAP 25% within the hour regardless of findings.
Emergency surgery based only on the BP number.
rationales: Correct. Severe hypertension without acute organ injury generally requires timely oral-treatment adjustment and follow-up rather than an automatic emergency infusion.
Incorrect. The number alone does not establish a hypertensive emergency.
Incorrect. First-hour IV targets apply to selected emergencies with acute organ injury.
Incorrect. A BP number alone does not identify a surgical indication.
questions.clue: Severe BP elevation without end-organ damage.
questions.priority: Manage hypertensive urgency appropriately.
questions.takeaway: Acute organ injury determines emergency treatment; otherwise arrange timely oral treatment and follow-up.

questions.stem: After repeat BP measurement and clinical evaluation, classify the anticipated management for these nonpregnant adults with severe hypertension.
rows: BP 188/122 mm Hg with headache and anxiety; exam otherwise normal
BP 204/128 mm Hg with new acute kidney injury
BP 196/126 mm Hg with papilledema
BP 184/121 mm Hg; dyspnea was evaluated, oxygenation is normal, and no acute cardiac or other organ injury is found
BP 210/130 mm Hg with signs of acute heart failure
rationales: No acute organ injury is found after evaluation; arrange timely oral treatment adjustment and close follow-up.
New AKI is acute target-organ injury and requires monitored emergency management.
Papilledema in this severe presentation requires urgent assessment and monitored emergency management.
Dyspnea was evaluated rather than assumed benign; without acute injury the oral-treatment/follow-up pathway is appropriate.
Acute heart failure is target-organ injury and requires hospital treatment tailored to the emergency.
questions.clue: Target organ damage, not the BP number, separates emergency from urgency.
questions.priority: Match level of care to hypertensive urgency or emergency.
questions.takeaway: Evaluate symptoms for acute organ injury; severe BP without injury does not require universal IV normalization or a fixed 24–48-hour normalization target.

questions.stem: A client at the clinic has a BP of 186/122 mm Hg, a headache and feels anxious. Repeat measurement and clinical evaluation find no acute target-organ injury. The client asks, "Am I going to end up in intensive care?" Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "There is nothing to worry about; your blood pressure is fine."
"Yes, you will need IV medicine to bring your pressure down within the hour."
"I can see you are worried. There are no signs of organ damage, so the plan is to lower your pressure gradually with pills."
"This is caused by your anxiety, so once you calm down it will be normal."
rationales: Severe BP elevation needs treatment and follow-up; dismissing it is false reassurance.
An immediate IV reduction is reserved for a clinically identified emergency, not the number alone.

Acknowledging concern and explaining timely oral-regimen adjustment, controlled reduction and follow-up is appropriate after evaluation excludes acute injury. There is no universal 24–48-hour normalization target.
Anxiety may coexist with hypertension; it does not establish the cause or eliminate the need for follow-up.
questions.clue: Severe BP without organ damage in a worried client.
questions.priority: Acknowledge anxiety and give accurate information about hypertensive urgency.
questions.takeaway: Acknowledge concern and explain the evaluated treatment plan; distinguish severe hypertension without acute injury from hypertensive emergency.

questions.stem: A client with a history of IV drug use has fever, a new murmur and splinter hemorrhages. Which diagnostic test should the nurse anticipate collecting first?
options: Troponin level to confirm myocarditis
Prompt blood-culture sets before antibiotics, when feasible
Endomyocardial biopsy
Ankle-brachial index
rationales: Troponin can identify myocardial injury but does not identify the bloodstream pathogen causing suspected endocarditis.

Fever, new murmur and embolic/vascular findings raise concern for IE. Obtain at least two, ideally three, adequately filled blood-culture sets promptly when feasible; do not delay urgent antibiotics in an unstable client.
Endomyocardial biopsy is not the first sampling test for this suspected infection.
ABI assesses limb arterial perfusion, not bloodstream infection.
questions.clue: IV drug use with fever, new murmur and splinter hemorrhages.
questions.priority: Obtain blood cultures in suspected endocarditis.
questions.takeaway: Obtain appropriate cultures promptly in suspected IE without creating a prolonged delay in urgent antibiotic treatment.

questions.stem: A client with pericarditis had sharp chest pain worse when lying flat and a friction rub. The nurse now notes JVD and a falling blood pressure. What should the nurse suspect?
options: Expected progression of uncomplicated pericarditis
Hypertensive emergency with end-organ damage
Cardiac tamponade from a pericardial effusion
Postural hypotension needing compression stockings
rationales: JVD with hypotension signals a complication, not expected progression.
The client is hypotensive, not severely hypertensive.
The book says to always assess for tamponade in pericarditis; low BP and JVD with effusion suggest it.
Postural hypotension measures do not address new JVD in pericarditis.
questions.clue: New JVD and hypotension develop in pericarditis.
questions.priority: Detect tamponade as a complication of pericarditis.

questions.stem: A client treated previously for infective endocarditis is scheduled for a dental extraction. What should the nurse anticipate?
options: Colchicine before the procedure
IVIG infusion before the procedure
Pericardiocentesis before the procedure
Prophylactic antibiotics before the procedure
rationales: Colchicine is listed for recurrent pericarditis.
IVIG is listed for select immune-mediated myocarditis.
Pericardiocentesis treats tamponade or large effusion.
The book lists prophylactic antibiotics before invasive procedures, including dental, for IE.
questions.clue: A prior IE client faces a dental extraction.
questions.priority: Prevent recurrent endocarditis around invasive procedures.

questions.stem: A client being treated for infective endocarditis related to injection drug use tells the nurse, "I want to stop using, but I don't know where to start." Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Explain that finishing the antibiotics is all that is needed to prevent recurrence
Tell the client that valve replacement will be needed if drug use continues
Change the topic to the antibiotic schedule to avoid upsetting the client
Arrange the addiction referral that is part of the treatment plan
rationales: Antibiotics treat the infection but do not address the drug use that caused it.
The book reserves valve replacement for antibiotic failure or prosthetic valve infection; using it as a threat is not therapeutic.
Avoiding the topic misses the client's readiness for help.
The book lists an addiction referral when IE is related to IV drug use.
questions.clue: The client voices readiness to stop injection drug use.
questions.priority: Support recovery from substance use with a referral.

questions.stem: A client has fever, a new heart murmur and splinter hemorrhages. Which question should the nurse ask, in a nonjudgmental way, to gather the most relevant history?
options: "Have you been around anyone with tuberculosis lately?"
"Have you injected any drugs or had dental work recently?"
"Does anyone in your family have high cholesterol?"
"Have you recently spent time at high altitude?"
rationales: TB is listed as an infectious cause of pericarditis, not endocarditis.
The book lists IV drug use and recent dental procedures in the assessment of infective endocarditis.
Family cholesterol history does not explain fever, a new murmur and splinter hemorrhages.
High altitude is listed as a cause of secondary pulmonary hypertension.
questions.clue: Fever, a new murmur and splinter hemorrhages suggest endocarditis.
questions.priority: Ask sensitively about drug use and dental procedures.

questions.stem: An ambulatory client has symptomatic orthostatic hypotension. Assessment finds no heart failure, advanced kidney disease or fluid/sodium restriction. Which nonpharmacological measures should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Start midodrine independently before evaluating reversible causes.
Teach leg-muscle counterpressure exercises and gradual position changes.
Restrict fluids solely to treat orthostatic dizziness.
Use a prescribed waist-high compression garment or abdominal binder.
Start fludrocortisone independently as the first nursing action.
Maintain the individualized fluid plan and discuss appropriate salt intake with the clinician.
rationales: Incorrect. Medication treatment requires a prescription and evaluation; it is not an independent first action.
Correct. Muscle counterpressure and slow position changes may reduce pooling and symptoms.
Incorrect. Fluid restriction without another indication can worsen volume depletion.
Correct. Appropriately prescribed compression can reduce venous pooling; hospital SCD devices are not interchangeable ambulatory therapy.
Incorrect. Fludrocortisone requires individualized assessment and monitoring.
Correct. Hydration and any salt increase depend on comorbidities and the prescribed plan; an electrolyte beverage is not mandatory.
questions.clue: The client has symptomatic postural hypotension with no treatment yet.
questions.priority: Start with non-drug comfort and safety measures.
questions.takeaway: Treat orthostatic symptoms with individualized non-drug measures and fall prevention; account for fluid and sodium restrictions.

questions.stem: A 70-kg client with myocarditis and suspected low-output heart failure is assessed for cardiogenic shock. Which findings support impaired perfusion and need prompt escalation? Select all that apply.
options: SBP 84 mm Hg sustained for 40 minutes.
Warm skin with brisk refill and no other new perfusion changes.
Urine output 20 mL/hour for the past 3 hours.
Lactate 3.1 mmol/L with worsening clinical perfusion.
Urine output 60 mL/hour with stable renal function.
SBP 98 mm Hg with stable mentation, output and other perfusion findings.
rationales: Correct. Sustained hypotension with the cardiac context supports shock concern.
Incorrect. These isolated reassuring findings do not establish shock.
Correct. Output is about 0.29 mL/kg/hour and is concerning with other hypoperfusion cues.
Correct. Elevated lactate plus deteriorating perfusion supports shock concern, though lactate is not specific to one cause.
Incorrect. The stated output/trend is reassuring for this client.
Incorrect. A BP value alone neither proves nor excludes shock; the described stable integrated assessment is less concerning.
questions.clue: The book says to monitor for cardiogenic shock in myocarditis.
questions.priority: Recognize the defining criteria of cardiogenic shock.
questions.takeaway: Diagnose shock from the combined hemodynamic and organ-perfusion assessment, not one isolated threshold.

questions.stem: Three diagnosed clients have specialist-directed plans: Client A has culture-confirmed susceptible infective endocarditis; Client B has selected immune-mediated myocarditis with persistent low-output heart failure; Client C has recurrent pericarditis. Match each prescribed intervention to the stated plan.
rows: Pathogen- and valve-specific IV antibiotic therapy.
Specialist-selected IVIG for the documented immune-mediated condition.
Colchicine for recurrent pericardial inflammation.
An appropriate prescribed NSAID for pericardial inflammation.
Monitored inotropic support for persistent low cardiac output.
rationales: IE antibiotic choice/dose depends on organism, susceptibility and valve context; an arbitrary penicillin regimen is not universal.
IVIG is specialist-selected for the specific immune-mediated case, not routine for all myocarditis.
Colchicine is used in selected pericarditis plans to reduce recurrence.
A prescribed NSAID may treat pericardial inflammation after contraindication assessment.
The myocarditis client has the explicitly supplied low-output indication; inotropes are not exclusive to myocarditis.
questions.clue: Each drug appears in one row of the treatment table.
questions.priority: Match anti-infective and anti-inflammatory drugs to their condition.
questions.takeaway: Match drugs to the supplied diagnosis, indication and prescription; a drug name alone does not uniquely identify a disease.

questions.stem: A client with pericarditis is being monitored. For each finding, indicate whether it is expected with pericarditis or requires immediate follow-up.
rows: Sharp chest pain that is worse when lying flat
Pericardial friction rub
Previously evaluated diffuse ST elevation consistent with the established pericarditis diagnosis
New JVD with a falling blood pressure
SBP below 90 mm Hg with urine output under 30 mL/h
rationales: Positional pleuritic pain is compatible with the established pericarditis diagnosis.
A pericardial friction rub is a characteristic finding.
The previously evaluated diffuse pattern can fit pericarditis; new focal ischemic changes or unexplained pain require reassessment.
New JVD and falling BP may indicate tamponade and require urgent assessment.
Hypotension with oliguria signals hypoperfusion. In pericardial tamponade the shock mechanism is obstructive; urgent evaluation and definitive treatment are required.
questions.clue: Hemodynamic changes separate complications from expected pericarditis findings.
questions.priority: Escalate signs of tamponade or shock in pericarditis.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old smoker reports calf pain when walking that is relieved by rest. The feet are cool and pale with diminished pulses. Which test does the nurse anticipate?
options: Ankle-brachial index
D-dimer blood test
Venous duplex ultrasound
CT pulmonary angiography
rationales: Claudication, cool pale skin and weak pulses point to arterial occlusive disease, and the book lists the ankle-brachial index (ABI) first among its diagnostic tests.
D-dimer is listed for venous occlusion.
Venous duplex is listed for DVT, not arterial disease.
CT pulmonary angiography is for suspected pulmonary embolism.
questions.clue: Claudication with cool, pale skin and weak pulses.
questions.priority: Recognize arterial occlusive disease and its diagnostic test.

questions.stem: A client has acute proximal lower-extremity DVT and active major bleeding that prevents anticoagulation. The team is considering temporary embolic protection. Which intervention should the nurse anticipate?
options: Starting heparin despite the contraindication
Placement of an IVC filter
Supervised exercise therapy
Revascularization with bypass surgery
rationales: Giving heparin despite active major bleeding would contradict the stated contraindication.
A retrievable IVC filter may be considered for acute proximal DVT when anticoagulation is absolutely contraindicated; reassess promptly and plan removal when anticoagulation becomes feasible.
An exercise program does not replace the needed acute VTE management.
Arterial bypass does not treat this proximal venous thrombus.
questions.clue: Anticoagulation is contraindicated in a DVT client.
questions.priority: Select an alternative DVT treatment when anticoagulants cannot be used.
questions.takeaway: Filter use is selective, generally for acute proximal VTE with an absolute anticoagulation contraindication, with a reassessment/removal plan.

questions.stem: After surgery and several days of bed rest, a client's lower leg is swollen, warm, red and tender. Which test does the nurse anticipate first?
options: Ankle-brachial index
Arterial angiography
Venous duplex ultrasound
Doppler arterial study for claudication
rationales: ABI evaluates arterial disease with cool, pale skin, not warm swelling.
Angiography is listed for arterial occlusive disease.
Swelling, warmth and redness after surgery and immobility suggest DVT; the book lists venous duplex ultrasound first among the tests for venous occlusion.
Claudication testing is for arterial disease, not venous occlusion.
questions.clue: Surgery and immobility with a warm, red, swollen leg.
questions.priority: Recognize DVT and its diagnostic test.

questions.stem: The nurse is screening a 70-year-old client for peripheral arterial occlusive disease (PAOD). Which factors in the client's history increase the risk? Select all that apply.
options: Pregnancy
Smoking
Inherited clotting disorder
Diabetes
Hyperlipidemia
Recent prolonged immobility
rationales: The book lists pregnancy as a risk factor for venous occlusion, not PAOD.
Smoking is a listed risk factor for arterial occlusive disease.
Inherited clotting disorders are listed for venous occlusion.
Diabetes is a listed risk factor for arterial occlusive disease.
Hyperlipidemia is a listed risk factor for arterial occlusive disease.
Prolonged immobility is listed as a venous (DVT) risk factor.
questions.clue: The screening is for arterial, not venous, disease.
questions.priority: Identify modifiable risk factors for PAOD.

questions.stem: A client with PAOD and claudication asks how to improve symptoms. Which measures in the treatment plan should the nurse reinforce? Select all that apply.
options: Exercise therapy
Compression stockings
Smoking cessation
Thrombolytic therapy
Statin therapy as prescribed
IVC filter placement
rationales: Exercise therapy is listed as a treatment for arterial occlusive disease.
Compression stockings are listed for venous occlusion.
Smoking cessation is the first listed treatment for arterial occlusive disease.
Thrombolytic therapy is listed for severe venous occlusion.
Statins are listed as a treatment for arterial occlusive disease.
An IVC filter is for DVT when anticoagulation is contraindicated.
questions.clue: The client has arterial, not venous, disease.
questions.priority: Reinforce lifestyle and drug measures for PAOD.

questions.stem: The nurse assesses clients with leg symptoms. For each finding, indicate whether it is more consistent with arterial occlusive disease or venous occlusion (DVT).
rows: Calf pain with walking that eases with rest
Warm, red, tender lower leg
Ulcer on a toe
Swelling of one lower limb
Cool, pale skin with diminished pulses
rationales: Claudication relieved by rest is listed for arterial disease.
Warm, red, tender skin is listed for venous occlusion.
Ulcers on toes or pressure points are listed for arterial disease.
Lower-limb swelling is listed for venous occlusion.
Cool, pale skin and diminished pulses are listed for arterial disease.
questions.clue: Perfusion versus congestion findings separate arterial from venous disease.
questions.priority: Differentiate arterial and venous occlusion by assessment.

questions.stem: The nurse on a vascular unit receives report on four clients. Which client should the nurse see first?
options: A client with DVT who suddenly reports shortness of breath
A client with PAOD whose calf pain after walking resolved with rest
A client with DVT with stable leg swelling awaiting warfarin teaching
A client with PAOD asking about a smoking cessation program
rationales: The book warns that pulmonary embolism is possible if a DVT thrombus dislodges; sudden dyspnea needs immediate assessment.
Claudication relieved by rest is an expected PAOD finding.
Stable swelling is an expected DVT finding.
Teaching about smoking cessation is important but not urgent.
questions.clue: Sudden shortness of breath in a client with DVT.
questions.priority: See first the client with a possible pulmonary embolism.

questions.stem: A client has acute proximal DVT. Which elements may be included in an individualized treatment plan? Select all that apply.
options: Routine arterial bypass for every venous thrombus.
Therapeutic anticoagulation when not contraindicated.
An arterial claudication exercise program instead of anticoagulation.
Prescribed compression for bothersome edema/pain after assessment.
Antiplatelet/statin treatment as a substitute for DVT anticoagulation.
A retrievable IVC filter if active major bleeding absolutely prevents anticoagulation.
rationales: Incorrect. Routine arterial bypass is not DVT treatment.
Correct. Anticoagulation limits clot extension and recurrent embolism.
Incorrect. An arterial exercise program is not a substitute for VTE treatment.
Correct. Compression may provide selected symptom relief; it is not routinely prescribed solely to prevent post-thrombotic syndrome.
Incorrect. These medicines may have other indications but do not replace therapeutic DVT anticoagulation.
Correct. This specified proximal-VTE/absolute-contraindication setting may warrant a temporary filter, with reassessment and removal planning.
questions.clue: The diagnosis is a venous thrombus.
questions.priority: Anticipate DVT treatments that prevent clot extension and embolism.
questions.takeaway: DVT treatment is individualized; distinguish symptom-directed compression from routine prevention claims.

questions.stem: After a femoral PCI on heparin, a client has a growing groin hematoma, a falling hemoglobin and hypotension. Which reversal agent does the nurse anticipate?
options: Vitamin K (phytonadione)
Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate
Idarucizumab
Protamine sulfate
rationales: Vitamin K reverses warfarin.

Four-factor PCC has selected major-bleeding reversal uses under a prescribed protocol; protamine is the specific reversal agent for the heparin in this case. Andexanet is not an available routine U.S. alternative after the 2025 cessation of U.S. sales.
Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran.
The book pairs heparin reversal with protamine sulfate.
questions.clue: Bleeding at the access site in a client on heparin.
questions.priority: Reverse the correct anticoagulant in post-PCI bleeding.

questions.stem: A client with advanced CKD is scheduled for angiography. The team has assessed renal risk and current volume status. Which nursing action best follows an individualized kidney-risk reduction plan?
options: Give indicated isotonic hydration and monitor for overload
Restrict fluids for 24 hours after the procedure
Request high-osmolar contrast agent
Check renal function once weekly
rationales: Hydration may be prescribed according to renal risk and volume status; it is not identical for every client with reduced kidney function. Monitor response and overload risk.
A universal 24-hour fluid restriction is not a kidney-protection plan and may worsen volume depletion.
High-osmolar contrast is not the preferred risk-reduction strategy.
Arrange renal monitoring according to the procedure/risk plan; a fixed once-weekly schedule may miss a clinically important change.
questions.clue: Contrast exposure in a client at renal risk.
questions.priority: Prevent contrast-induced nephropathy.
questions.takeaway: Reduce kidney risk using the prescribed contrast/hydration plan and individualized volume assessment; do not assume every post-contrast AKI is caused by contrast.

questions.stem: Two days after coronary stenting, a client reports recurrent chest pain and the ECG shows new ischemic changes. What should the nurse suspect?
options: Contrast-induced acute kidney injury
Stent thrombosis needing urgent angioplasty
Expected access-site discomfort
Post-procedure infection at the site
rationales: AKI presents with reduced urine output and elevated creatinine.
Recurrent chest pain with ischemic ECG changes are the book's signs of stent thrombosis, managed with emergency angioplasty if acute.
Access-site problems show bruising or swelling, not ischemic ECG changes.
Infection shows fever, erythema and drainage, not ischemic ECG changes.
questions.clue: Recurrent chest pain with ischemic ECG changes after stenting.
questions.priority: Recognize stent thrombosis as an emergency.

questions.stem: Two days after a cardiac procedure, a client has a fever and redness at the catheter site. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Maintain sterile technique with site care
Wait for culture results before giving any antibiotic
Monitor temperature and site redness
Start empirical antibiotics as prescribed, pending cultures
Use clean rather than sterile technique to save time
rationales: The book lists maintaining sterile technique post-op in infection management.
The book says to start empirical antibiotics pending cultures, not to wait.
Monitoring for fever and site redness is listed management.
The book lists starting empirical antibiotics pending cultures.
The book calls for sterile technique.
questions.clue: Fever and site redness after an invasive line.
questions.priority: Prevent and treat infection after cardiac intervention.

questions.stem: After cardiac catheterization, which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A client with a small, stable bruise at the radial site
A client asking how long to take aspirin and clopidogrel
A client whose right leg is suddenly painful, pale and pulseless
A client due for a daily creatinine check after contrast
rationales: A small stable bruise is not an acute threat.
Medication questions are important but not urgent.
The book describes sudden pain, pallor and pulselessness as arterial occlusion and an emergency.
Daily renal monitoring is routine follow-up.
questions.clue: Sudden pain, pallor and pulselessness in a limb.
questions.priority: Treat acute arterial occlusion as an emergency.

questions.stem: The nurse monitors clients after cardiac intervention. For each finding, indicate the complication it most likely signals.
rows: Palpitations and syncope with new atrial fibrillation
Reduced urine output and a rising creatinine
Recurrent chest pain with ischemic ECG changes
Frequent PVCs on the monitor
columns: Acute kidney injury after the procedure
rationales: The book lists palpitations, syncope and ECG changes such as atrial fibrillation as arrhythmia signs.

Oliguria and rising creatinine indicate concern for AKI after the procedure. Contrast association does not prove contrast causation; assess bleeding, perfusion, medications, obstruction and other causes.
Recurrent chest pain and ischemic ECG changes are the signs of stent thrombosis or restenosis.
PVCs are listed as an example ECG change with post-intervention arrhythmias.
questions.clue: Each finding matches one complication's listed signs.
questions.priority: Recognize early signs of post-intervention complications.

questions.stem: A client has sudden pain, pallor and pulselessness in the left leg after a catheter-based procedure. While the provider is being notified, how should the nurse position the limb?
options: Elevate the leg on two pillows
Dangle the leg over the side of the bed
Raise the foot of the bed with the knee gatch
Keep the leg flat
rationales: Elevation is the book's advice for venous (DVT) occlusion, not arterial occlusion.
The book directs keeping the limb flat, not dependent.
Raising the leg is not the positioning the book gives for arterial occlusion.
The book states that for arterial occlusion the limb is kept flat and treated as an emergency.
questions.clue: Pain, pallor and pulselessness point to arterial occlusion.
questions.priority: Position the limb correctly in acute arterial occlusion.

questions.stem: A client has returned from cardiac surgery. Which assessments should the nurse include to detect complications early? Select all that apply.
options: Discontinue cardiac monitoring once the client is awake
Chest tube output
Signs of Beck's triad
Delay wound inspection until the day of discharge
Serum electrolytes
rationales: The book says to watch for dysrhythmias after cardiac surgery, so monitoring continues.
The book directs monitoring chest tube output.
The book lists tamponade (Beck's triad) among post-cardiac surgery risks.
The book lists infection as a post-surgery risk, so the wound needs ongoing inspection.
The book directs monitoring electrolytes.
questions.clue: The client is newly post-op from cardiac surgery.
questions.priority: Monitor for the major post-cardiac surgery risks.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing cardiac concepts while caring for clients. For each description, indicate whether it describes preload or afterload.
rows: The volume of blood filling the heart before it contracts
The resistance the heart must overcome to eject blood
Like tying a balloon's neck tighter, which makes air harder to push out
Rises as incoming blood stretches the heart, like filling a balloon
The pressure the heart faces after contraction starts
rationales: The book defines preload as the volume before the squeeze, the blood that fills the heart before it contracts.
Afterload is the resistance the heart must overcome to eject blood ("pressure to push against").
The book compares afterload to a tightly tied balloon neck: the tighter it is, the harder it is to push air out.
The book says the amount of blood filling the heart (balloon) increases as it stretches, which is preload.
The book's memory tip is "Afterload = After-push," the resistance faced after contraction starts.
questions.clue: Preload is volume coming in; afterload is resistance to ejection.
questions.priority: Distinguish preload (pre-fill volume) from afterload (after-push resistance).

questions.stem: The nurse wants to assess a client's S1 heart sound, which marks the beginning of systole. Where should the nurse place the stethoscope to hear S1 best?
options: At the apex, 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line
At the base, 2nd intercostal space, right sternal border
At the base, 2nd intercostal space, left sternal border
At the 3rd intercostal space, left midaxillary line
rationales: The book states S1 (mitral and tricuspid closure) is heard best at the apex, 5th ICS, midclavicular line.
The 2nd ICS at the right sternal border is part of the base, where the book says S2 is heard best.
The 2nd ICS at the left sternal border is also the base, the best site for S2 rather than S1.
The midaxillary line is not the site the book gives for hearing S1.
questions.clue: S1 is produced by mitral and tricuspid closure.
questions.priority: Auscultate each heart sound at the site where it is loudest.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches a client with hypertension how high blood pressure affects the heart's workload. Which client statement shows the teaching was effective?
options: "High blood pressure mainly increases how much blood fills my heart before it squeezes."
"When my pressure is high, my heart has to push harder against more resistance to pump blood out."
"Afterload is the amount of blood coming into my heart from my veins."
"My heart only meets resistance before it starts to contract."
rationales: The volume filling the heart before it contracts is preload, not the resistance raised by high blood pressure.
Afterload is the resistance the heart must overcome to eject blood; higher pressure means more resistance to push against.
Blood coming into the heart describes preload ("pre-fill"), not afterload.
The book describes afterload as the resistance faced after contraction starts ("after-push").
questions.clue: The client links high pressure to the resistance the heart pushes against.
questions.priority: Confirm the client understands afterload as resistance to ejection.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the histories of several clients. Which conditions place a client at risk for cardiac tamponade? Select all that apply.
options: Kidney failure with uremia
Heart rupture after a recent MI
Iron-deficiency anemia
Systemic lupus erythematosus
Seasonal allergic rhinitis
Blunt chest trauma from a car crash
rationales: The book lists kidney failure (uremia) as a cause of tamponade.
Heart rupture after MI or surgery is listed as a cause.
Anemia is not among the causes the book lists.
Autoimmune diseases such as SLE and RA are listed causes.
Allergic rhinitis is not a listed cause.
Blunt or penetrating trauma is a listed cause.
questions.clue: Uremia, post-MI rupture, autoimmune disease and chest trauma all appear on the causes list.
questions.priority: Identify clients at risk so tamponade is recognized early.

questions.stem: Before pericardiocentesis, a client with cardiac tamponade had a BP of 82/64 mm Hg, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds and pulsus paradoxus. For each finding after the procedure, indicate whether it suggests the tamponade is resolving or persisting.
rows: BP 112/70 mm Hg with a wider pulse pressure
Neck veins are no longer distended
Systolic BP still drops 14 mm Hg during inspiration
Electrical alternans persists on the ECG
Heart sounds are now clearly audible
rationales: Hypotension and a narrow pulse pressure are tamponade signs; a higher BP with a wider pulse pressure shows improvement.
Elevated CVP with JVD is part of Beck's triad; flat neck veins suggest the compression is relieved.
A drop of more than 10 mm Hg in BP during inspiration is pulsus paradoxus, a sign of ongoing tamponade.
Electrical alternans is listed as a tamponade sign, so its persistence suggests ongoing compression.
Muffled heart sounds are part of Beck's triad; clear heart sounds suggest the fluid has been removed.
questions.clue: Compare each finding with the tamponade signs present before the procedure.
questions.priority: Evaluate pericardiocentesis by the resolution of Beck's triad and related signs.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for four clients on a cardiac step-down unit. Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A client with lupus who reports mild joint stiffness this morning
A client with chronic kidney failure awaiting a scheduled dialysis session
A client 2 days after an MI who is newly hypotensive with JVD and muffled heart sounds
A client on an anticoagulant whose latest coagulation result is in the target range
rationales: Lupus is a risk factor, but mild joint stiffness is not a sign of tamponade.
Uremia is a risk factor, but this client has no signs of instability.
Hypotension, JVD and muffled heart sounds (Beck's triad) after MI suggest tamponade from heart rupture, a true emergency.
Anticoagulants are a risk factor, but a therapeutic result with no symptoms is not urgent.
questions.clue: Beck's triad has appeared in a client after MI.
questions.priority: See first the client with signs of a life-threatening emergency.

questions.stem: After PCI for STEMI, which findings support successful reperfusion when considered together? Select all that apply.
options: ST-segment elevation substantially resolves.
The client’s ischemic chest pain resolves.
Angiography documents restored flow through the treated artery.
ST elevation increases with worsening chest pain.
The client develops new hemodynamic instability.
Troponin rises without any clinical, ECG or angiographic context.
rationales: Correct. ST resolution supports improved myocardial perfusion.
Correct. Pain relief supports a favorable clinical response but is interpreted with objective data.
Correct. Restored angiographic flow directly supports opening of the treated vessel.
Incorrect. These findings raise concern for ongoing ischemia or a complication.
Incorrect. New instability requires urgent assessment rather than being treated as a reassuring response.
Incorrect. Biomarker elevation reflects myocardial injury and cannot independently prove successful reperfusion.
questions.clue: ST resolution, pain relief and a sudden biomarker rise follow successful reopening.
questions.priority: Evaluate PCI by the signs of reperfusion.
questions.takeaway: Assess reperfusion using the clinical response, ECG and coronary-flow findings; troponin change alone is not proof.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews 12-lead ECGs and angiogram reports for clients with acute MI. For each finding, indicate the MI location it most likely reflects.
rows: ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF
ST elevation in leads V1-V4
ST elevation in leads I, aVL, V5 and V6
Occlusion of the right coronary artery
rationales: The book maps leads II, III and aVF to the inferior wall.
Leads V1-V4 reflect the anterior wall.
Leads I, aVL, V5 and V6 reflect the lateral wall.
The book states the inferior wall is supplied by the right coronary artery (RCA).
questions.clue: Each lead group views a specific region of the heart.
questions.priority: Correlate lead changes with the affected region.

questions.stem: During femoral sheath removal after PCI, a client's heart rate drops to 46/min and BP falls to 84/50 mm Hg. The nurse recognizes a vasovagal response. Which actions does the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
options: Give atropine as prescribed for the bradycardia
Increase the nitroglycerin infusion
Give a fluid bolus as prescribed
Hold nitrates, which reduce preload
Maintain prescribed access-site compression until hemostasis according to protocol
Release pressure on the site to help raise the BP
rationales: The book says to give atropine if the client becomes bradycardic during sheath removal.
Nitrates reduce preload and worsen hypotension; the book says to hold them.
A fluid bolus is part of the book's response to vasovagal hypotension.
The book says to hold nitrates (preload reducers) during this response.
Compression is maintained until hemostasis using the access-site protocol and ordered device; duration depends on anticoagulation, sheath size and the client’s response.
Releasing pressure risks bleeding; the book calls for pressure, a C-clamp or a FemoStop.
questions.clue: Bradycardia and hypotension during sheath removal signal a vasovagal response.
questions.priority: Support HR and BP while keeping the access site from bleeding.

questions.stem: A client with chest pain and suspected NSTEMI is being evaluated, and the provider also suspects aortic dissection. The standing ACS protocol includes non-enteric-coated aspirin STAT. Which action by the nurse is best?
options: Give the aspirin, since every NSTEMI requires it
Give enteric-coated aspirin instead to protect the stomach
Give half the aspirin dose and reassess the pain in 1 hour
Hold the aspirin and clarify the prescription with the provider
rationales: Aspirin is not given when aortic dissection is suspected, even with NSTEMI.
The book calls for non-enteric-coated aspirin when it is given; changing the form does not address the contraindication.
Reducing the dose does not remove the risk; the drug should be held and clarified.
The book lists suspected aortic dissection as an exception to STAT aspirin, so the nurse should hold and clarify.
questions.clue: Aortic dissection is suspected.
questions.priority: Recognize contraindications before giving STAT aspirin.

questions.stem: A client with ACS used cocaine 1 hour ago and is agitated and hypertensive with chest pain. Which medications does the nurse anticipate in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: A benzodiazepine for agitation
Nitrates for chest pain and hypertension
A pure beta-blocker such as metoprolol
A calcium channel blocker if vasospasm is refractory
No chest pain medication until the cocaine wears off
rationales: The book says to treat agitation, hypertension and pain with benzodiazepines first.
Nitrates are given first along with benzodiazepines.

During active stimulant intoxication, clarify a pure beta-blocker order and follow the acute chest-pain protocol. Unopposed alpha activity is a concern rather than a proven universal outcome; combined alpha/beta agents may be considered by the treating clinician in selected circumstances.
Calcium channel blockers are added if vasospasm is refractory.
The book directs active treatment of pain and hypertension; delaying care is not appropriate.
questions.clue: The ACS is driven by acute cocaine effect.
questions.priority: Choose drugs that treat cocaine-related ACS without unopposed alpha stimulation.
questions.takeaway: Active stimulant intoxication requires prompt treatment of agitation, vasospasm and ACS; do not apply a blanket beta-blocker ban to every client with a cocaine history.

questions.stem: A client’s discharge plan after MI prescribes aspirin 81 mg daily, continued unless the cardiology team changes the plan. Which statements show understanding?
rows: “I will continue aspirin unless my prescribing team changes the plan.”
“I will take the prescribed 81 mg dose each day.”
“I can add ibuprofen for knee pain without checking with my team.”
“Aspirin reduces platelet aggregation.”
“I will stop aspirin when cardiac rehabilitation ends.”
rationales: Follow the individualized antiplatelet plan; do not stop on your own.
Low-dose maintenance aspirin is prescribed here; larger doses should not be substituted independently.
Ibuprofen may interfere with aspirin and increase cardiovascular or bleeding risk; discuss safer pain treatment. There is no universal six-week point when NSAIDs become safe.
Aspirin irreversibly inhibits platelet activity, reducing arterial thrombosis risk.
